opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the two are actually quite connected. Small models are where you get the efficiency: they're cheap to run, fast, and you can deploy them on the edge or on-premise, which matters a lot to our customers. But the reasoning capabilities, the knowledge, and the ability to handle complex multi-step tasks still scale with compute. If you want to push the frontier on what these systems can actually do, you need to train larger models.

There's also a very practical reason. The large models are what make the small models good. You use them to generate data, to distill, to evaluate, to create the training signal that lets a 7-billion-parameter model punch well above its weight. So if you only ever trained small models, you'd eventually hit a ceiling, because you wouldn't have the teacher.

And then there's the market reality. Some use cases genuinely require the most capable model available: hard reasoning, coding, agentic workflows where errors compound. Enterprises want a portfolio. They want the big model for the hard tasks and the small model for the high-volume, latency-sensitive ones. Being able to offer both, and to let people move between them easily, is a big part of the value.

So our approach has always been to be very compute-efficient and to get the most out of every FLOP. That doesn't mean staying small. It means that when we do go big, we do it in a way that's efficient and that feeds back into the whole family of models.

r001.rationale: It says reasoning capabilities scale with compute and that pushing the frontier requires training larger models.

r002.rationale: It says large models make small models better by generating data, distilling, and providing training signals.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the two things are actually not in tension. They're linked, and in a pretty concrete way.

The first reason is that you can't make a very good small model without having a bigger one. The way you get a 7B model that behaves like a 30B model from two years ago is partly data, partly architecture, but a lot of it is that you have a stronger model you can use to generate, filter, and verify training data, and to distill from. So the frontier model is upstream of the small model. If you stop training at the top, your small models plateau pretty quickly.

The second reason is more about what the models are for. There's a class of tasks, say reasoning over a long context, planning, agentic workflows where the model has to call tools and recover from mistakes, where capability still scales with compute. We see it in our own training runs. And that's where a lot of enterprise value sits, so if we don't have a model that's competitive at that level, we're not really in the conversation with those customers. The small models cover latency-sensitive and cost-sensitive deployments, things running on-prem or at the edge, and that's a huge market too. But you need both ends.

And then the third thing, which is maybe less obvious, is that the research you do at scale teaches you things you then push down. Mixture of experts is a good example. We did it first with Mixtral at a relatively modest size, but the understanding of how to train it well came from pushing the scale. Same thing with how you do RL, how you handle very long contexts. Most of those techniques are developed on big runs and then become cheap enough to apply everywhere.

So I'd put it this way: the small models are the product most people touch, and the large models are how we make sure those products keep getting better. We're a small team compared to the US labs, so we have to be efficient about it, which is honestly why we're so focused on compute efficiency in the first place. But opting out of the frontier would mean opting out of the thing that makes efficiency possible.

r001.rationale: It says reasoning, long-context planning, and agentic task capability still scales with compute, supporting the need to train larger models for stronger reasoning performance.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says a strong small model depends on having a bigger model to generate, filter, and verify training data and to distill from.

astra-6.text:
The two are quite complementary. If you want to make a very good small model, you need to understand what makes a larger model work. Training at larger scale lets you explore capabilities that may not appear in smaller models, and then you can work on bringing those capabilities down to a much smaller computational budget, through better training methods and distillation.

The small models are very important because, in practice, people care about cost, latency, and where they can deploy them. But if you only train small models, you’re limiting what you can learn about how to improve them. So we see pushing larger models and making smaller models more efficient as two parts of the same research effort.

r001.rationale: The response says larger-scale training can reveal capabilities absent in smaller models, but it does not state that greater reasoning capabilities require larger models.

r002.rationale: The response says studying larger models helps make very good small models and describes bringing larger-model capabilities down through better training methods and distillation.

sol-6.1.text:
Because training large models is also how you learn to make better small models. At a smaller scale, you can run a lot of experiments, but you don’t necessarily know which improvements will carry over as you scale up. You need to explore that frontier yourself.

And there’s a very practical connection: a more capable large model can help you improve smaller models through the data it generates and through distillation. So we see these as complementary efforts. We want to push capabilities at the high end, and then bring as much of that intelligence as possible into models that are cheaper and faster to run.

r001.rationale: The response says larger models help push capabilities and transfer intelligence, but does not state that greater reasoning capabilities require larger models.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says training large models is how you learn to make better small models, and describes improving them through generated data and distillation.
